toc.title: The parts of life shutdown touches

sections.title: Work, school, hobbies, and physical health

toc.title: What it looks like on a real day
Use the energy when it's there

blocks.p: This is the third part of my Shutdown Experiences Survey results. Here you'll hear from real people in shutdown about the impact of shutdown on their daily lives, and about what helps and what doesn't. I hope you feel more validated and more normalized, and I hope you gain some language for your own experiences. A huge thank you to the people who took the survey and shared their own words.
The first question was: how often does shutdown affect your daily activities? There were four options: rarely, sometimes, often, and almost always.

Think of shutdown as a gradient. It's not all or nothing. Nobody exists purely in shutdown or purely not in shutdown. On an evolutionary level, shutdown can look like passing out and playing dead, but day to day, we don't really do that. We do live in some amount of shutdown, though, probably enough to feel disconnected: numb from our emotions, disconnected from other people, with negative thinking and feeling worthless. None of the Polyvagal states are completely on at all times. Each state is a gradient, and we have all of the states active at all times.
So if shutdown is active enough, it's going to affect your daily life in a noticeable way. How much depends on the person, and on how far down that gradient they've gone into shutdown.

ul: Rarely was the least common, at about 10 percent. This indicates a more functional shutdown. This person is probably noticing that they're more disconnected, maybe not feeling super motivated in life, but they're able to go to work, be a parent, and maintain some kind of relationships. They're just not getting much fulfillment out of life.
Almost always was at 25 percent. A quarter of the 77 people who responded said shutdown affects their daily life almost always.

blocks.p: So over half of the respondents said shutdown is a consistent, I would say chronic, part of their daily life.

blocks.h: The parts of life shutdown touches

blocks.p: The next question was: how does shutdown affect your daily life? People could pick as many areas of life as were relevant to them.
At the top, at 85 percent each, were mental health and personal relationships.

Along with shutdown come shame, guilt, sadness, emptiness, isolation, loneliness, hopelessness, difficulty thinking, and feeling worthless. If that's your day-to-day experience, it's definitely going to affect your mental health.

We need connection with others. We're a social species. We have to interact with each other to have more fulfilling lives, and, let's be honest, just to feel better. When we interact with each other and get safety cues like smiles, eye squints, and gentle touch, that's called co-regulation. Those cues activate our own safety system, and that improves us on a biological level. It affects our "health, growth, and restoration," as Dr. Stephen Porges so often says. So it's not just that it feels good. We need each other on a very biological level.

Shutdown is pretty much the opposite of that. All the defensive states, flight, fight, shutdown, and freeze, involve some disconnection. Shutdown might be the most disconnected, especially if it's a chronic, day in, day out experience. On top of that, shutdown disconnects us from our bodies. We sort of exist from the neck up. We're very disconnected from our emotions, our sensations, and our impulses from the bottom up. We're more familiar with our thoughts, and those are very negative.

Shutdown is definitely going to affect your personal relationships too, because in shutdown you don't really want to be with anyone. There's an impulse, a need, a desire to isolate, because when you isolate there's less stimulation. You can be alone. You can stay in bed with the lights off. You don't have to interact with anyone. You don't have to have the precious little energy you have sucked out of you by interactions with other people, or by overstimulation.

What can help is to give yourself what you need from shutdown. It's okay to be alone. We just don't want to be alone in bed forever. Give yourself moments of solitude: not isolation, where you're cutting people out of your life, but solitude, where you give yourself lower stimulation, mindfully experience a little of what it's like to be in shutdown, and then use your senses to slowly come out of it.

And we do have to connect with people, or pets. So give yourself some solitude, but connect with the people in your life who are connectable. Maybe there's someone you already have a relationship with. Reconnecting might seem overwhelming, but is there a way to express appreciation, or just say hi? Something that gives you a little connection to help you come out of shutdown.

blocks.h3: Work, school, hobbies, and physical health

blocks.p: In the middle, at around 64 to 67 percent, were work and school performance, hobbies or interests, and physical health. Motivation and focus are very low in shutdown, and I think that's what these have in common.

Motivation requires some mobilization, which means you can't really be in a dominant shutdown state. You have to have some access to flight and fight. But we don't want it out of control. We need flight and fight plus our safety state active at the same time. If you're mobilized, but you're able to focus it in a specific direction, that, to me, is motivation. And that's what we'd use on work, school, hobbies, and exercise.

In shutdown, there's really no motivation to study, or to work on your professional development and get that advancement in your career. And not only is there no motivation, there's potentially no interest. It's just not exciting. It's not intriguing. There's no curiosity in it. You're just existing day in, day out, without any spark within you to grow at work or at school. Students don't care about what's being taught to them. They're present, but they don't have any personal investment in it. They don't see the point. And it's not just students. In the workplace too: what's the point? I'm just here. I'm existing.
There's also no hope, because hope requires good access to our safety state. When you don't have hope or motivation, interest or focus, these areas of your life are going to be really challenging.

It's the same with hobbies or interests. There's no energy. There's no passion. The things that used to give you pleasure may not give you happiness anymore. If you don't have energy or interest, then hobbies are like, well, what's the point?

With physical health, it's easier not to eat well in shutdown. Maybe that's because there's less actual hunger. You're simply not feeling that bottom-up experience of hunger. People might also use binge eating as a way to cope with shutdown, or with coming out of shutdown, or with the potential to come out of it.

The first thing we do when we come out of shutdown is go into fight or flight, fight first. But the sensation of coming up the Polyvagal ladder into fight can be really overwhelming. You go from a state of emptiness to all of a sudden having energy in your system, and it probably feels like irritation or aggression. We tend to use that energy through some negative coping mechanism, some behavioral adaptation, so we might turn to things like binge eating. That's how shutdown could contribute to a more negative experience of physical health.

blocks.h: What it looks like on a real day

blocks.p: I asked people to share an example of when shutdown recently affected their daily life. I got a ton of responses and tried my best to whittle them down, but the words people used are fantastic. The themes that came up again and again: canceling plans, being alone, tiredness, sleep, guilt, regret, feeling worse, and disconnection from others, like work, friends, and partners.
Someone who's been in shutdown for four to ten years:

q: When I'm in an acute form of shutdown state, I stop moving at all for hours at a time. So I don't get anything done, not even getting a glass of water for myself, which often makes me feel guilty about not doing anything useful afterwards.

blocks.p: Another person, also four to ten years:

q: I just remember the day fading away. It was like I was on autopilot once I was able to move again, going through the bare minimum to get me to the end of the day. I ended up canceling plans with family and vaguely remember doing something for work that had to be done, but not doing the rest of my job. Even at the end of the day, when I was trying to come out of it, I wasn't fully present.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for 21 to 30 years:

q: I was due to go away for a romantic evening with my partner. I had felt myself going into shutdown, the heavy sinking feeling and cloud around my eyes. I felt feelings of self loathing creeping in and a desire to isolate and hide in my room (which is my safe space). I didn't fight it and instead sat with it, but it was dark and heavy and I ended up pushing away my partner, politely and with explanation, when he offered to come hug me, and cancelling our night away, as I knew I needed to be by myself until my safety state was accessible again for me to let people in/close to me. He cannot understand my process despite me explaining every step of the way, and as a result, it has driven a wedge between us, which I cannot seem to bridge.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for 31 to 40 years:

q: The last big shutdown left me immobile in bed for two days, isolated in the dark. It was almost an out of body experience. I couldn't hold the thought, and it felt like a whole body migraine. All I could do was lie in bed and twitch. No work got done, could barely talk. I did bodily maintenance things, but that was it.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for over 50 years:

q: Spending an ordinary afternoon hanging out with my child, crafting, sharing fun TV, and I realize I have disappeared. I'm going through the motions, but I am not even aware that she's in the room with me anymore. The TV has faded to the background. I'm empty. I'm missing life, the ordinary, and the extraordinary.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for four to ten years:

q: The most recent was in the last few weeks. My youngest daughter, who is studying for her high school diploma in performing arts, was due to return from a school trip to Euro Disney, where she had auditioned to take part in the end of season show. She was returning to where we live at approximately 1-2 AM. And having already entered shutdown prior to her leaving, I did not know what day it was that I was supposed to pick her up. Leaving her to make her way home alone in the early hours of the morning.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for 31 to 40 years:

q: I cancelled everything I had to do, moved deadlines, just so I could sleep the entire day. The next day, I did the same.

blocks.p: And someone in shutdown for less than a year:

q: This question alone is too much. Clicking boxes up until this point was manageable, but having to describe and recall, justify my own experiences takes me right back into shutdown.

blocks.p: Next I asked: how do you cope with this? What are your ways of dealing with shutdown day in, day out? These weren't checkboxes. These are the actual words of people in shutdown.

A heads-up: some of these are really good pictures of what self-regulation could look like for you moving forward, and some are on the more dysfunctional side. I included them because I want you to have an accurate look at what shutdown, and dealing with shutdown, can look like for real people.
Someone in shutdown for 11 to 20 years:

q: Listening to shamanic music, and moving my body to the music, starting slow, following the music when it gets faster, stomping my feet on the ground, crying, feeling angry, making fists, whatever my body wants to do until I suddenly feel better and lighter. It makes me smile every time I get out of dorsal vagal, through movement, back to ventral vagal. I feel hope and powerful. It feels incredibly good. "I can do it," is what goes through my mind. Then I feel a lot of love towards myself and may still move to the music holding/hugging myself. It's beautiful. My mind is calm then too. I can breathe more deeply. It feels comfortable to be in my body.

blocks.p: That's an awesome example of going from shutdown all the way to ventral. I'm assuming this took a lot of practice. It's not something someone in shutdown should expect to happen right away. It's technically possible, I guess, but it's not super realistic if you're just starting out. This is a process of practice, of building the strength of your safety state.
Someone in shutdown for 11 to 30 years:

q: What works best for me is to stop trying to stop it. Instead, I turn inward and ask my body what it needs/wants to do. I listen and then follow what it says.

blocks.p: This is probably more realistic for someone starting the process. As you build the strength of your safety state, you can recognize what it feels like to be in shutdown. You can allow it, and experience it from safety. You might just notice there's more capacity to be okay with being in shutdown. It won't be this out of control, isolated, dysfunctional thing. Instead, it turns into stillness. Safety plus shutdown at the same time equals stillness, and stillness is just sitting in the present moment and allowing all of your experiences, including the shutdown ones. Again, that's not easy, and it's probably not going to happen right away if you're just starting. But as you build the strength of your safety state, this becomes much more approachable.
Someone in shutdown for four to ten years:

q: I seem to be able to force myself out of a shutdown when I really need to, like when I'm going to work. When I'm really in acute shutdown, my go to is hurting myself, which provides a strong enough physical sensation to snap out of it. However, this does result in me pushing down the defensive energy instead of regulating it, which means that it always catches up with me at some point. So that's definitely not something I recommend, apart from obviously not wanting anyone to be hurt, even by themselves. What recently has worked for me is giving in to the need to crawl into a corner and disconnect from the world and all the external stimuli. Sometimes that's enough to ease back into my body by myself. Sometimes I need a safe other, my partner, to co-regulate with me. He doesn't consciously do anything to do that, apart from making himself available. Just being there in the room with me, sometimes checking in with me or asking a question, but more often just reading a book or doing something else that relaxes him and doesn't pressure me.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for less than a year:

q: Forcing myself to exercise doesn't work, but going to AA meetings does work. That's where I feel safe and not tired at all.

blocks.p: Someone in shutdown for one to three years: "What works is going outside and laying in the sun."
Someone in shutdown for over 50 years:

q: Long, slow breathing. My mantra: "I know who I am. I know my motives. I understand my issues and they are not my fault. I know what I am seeing and what I think about it. I will look after me."

blocks.p: And another person in shutdown for one to three years:

q: Calling my mom hasn't worked for me. It seems that she doesn't understand or feels tremendous guilt when she hears about my lived experiences. And that's okay. Calling a helpline has worked, but I only called during the times when I was in a very severe state of shutdown, when my thoughts got way too scary for me.

blocks.p: Then I asked: how do you change your daily routine to deal with shutdown? On a practical level, what are you doing differently day to day?

The themes that came up: allowing shutdown with less judgment or none, connection with others that's tolerable, structure, and movement. My recommendation is to start somewhere. Don't worry about doing all of these. Pick one that's approachable, start there, and build on it.
Someone in shutdown for over 50 years:

q: I have altered my daily routine to minimize contact with people whenever I have had the power to do so. This accommodates shutdown, I know. Yet feels beneficial because I've given myself room to maneuver around possible threats from spontaneous human contact. Solitude lets me concentrate and truly enjoy what I'm engaged with.

blocks.p: Another person:

q: I think to prevent shutdown and to work to move out of it, I've had to create a very rigid life structure and specifically a very rigid exercise routine. I am currently loosening things up and adjusting my daily habits or routines, but the entire three plus previous years have been very strict and not accommodating to any other change because "I need to work out at that time." Part of why I had this structure was that I knew that not moving could keep me in shutdown and I wanted to move out of shutdown, so I spent years with the rigid schedule to prevent me from being kept in shutdown.

blocks.p: For people starting to come out of shutdown, a very strict daily schedule is sometimes helpful. It might not be exercise. It could be: this is the time I get out of bed. I have to brush my teeth, shower, comb my hair, and get dressed. I've got to do these basics. That might be the starting point. It's not forever. If you can get those down, maybe there's another thing you can add, like a daily walk. Setting some kind of structure you know you can follow is pretty common for someone in shutdown.
And someone in shutdown for one to three years:

q: Being around people before shutdown is good to prevent it from happening again. Being open with my feelings and having a person to talk to who gets it.

blocks.p: The last question was: how effective are your current strategies? This wasn't about ranking any one strategy. It was about how effective, in general, people feel their ways of dealing with shutdown are.

ul: 75 percent said their strategies are slightly to moderately effective.
20 percent said they don't have strategies, or they're not effective at all.
Only 14 percent said their strategies are very effective.

blocks.p: The takeaway, I think, is that you're probably not alone in your frustration with being stuck in shutdown. Other people are experiencing some frustration too, and maybe some hope. Lots of people in shutdown are trying lots of things to deal with it. There really is no one solution to shutdown. There's a bunch of things you can try.

blocks.h: Use the energy when it's there

blocks.p: So be persistent with the energy you do have. I know it's probably not a whole lot. But when it shows up, use it for something tolerable, maybe something you actually have a little interest in, instead of a behavioral adaptation like doom scrolling. Here's how that can go, depending on what you have available:

ol: Do something different. If you find yourself doom scrolling on your phone, that's a really good time to use that energy, that activation. Go out for a walk. Start a new hobby, research something you might be interested in, brainstorm. Try something different. If you hate it, stop doing it, and try something different the next day. Focus on what works and cut out what doesn't.

Bring mindfulness to it. If you can get that far, stopping one thing and doing something else like going for a walk, that's the perfect time for a little more mindfulness. Connect to the present moment as best you can through your senses. Notice what colors there are. Notice what the sun or the breeze feels like on your skin. Notice the sounds around you. If you can bring someone with you, like a partner, a spouse, or a friend, great. Or maybe it's the perfect time to take your dog for a walk.
If walking is too much, connect. That might be a really good time to connect with someone in a way that feels tolerable and approachable for you. That could be a pet.

If that's too much, put the phone down. It's totally okay to just put your phone down. Take a deep breath. Use your senses to connect with the environment you're in right now. What color is grabbing your attention? What sound? Take a deep breath, tell yourself you did a good job, and do it again later that day or the next day.

blocks.p: This is how you slowly come out of shutdown.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.
